name: Liberal corporatism
summary: Liberal corporatism keeps a market economy and individual liberty but organises economic life through bargaining among employers, workers and the state as social partners, with minimal state direction. It treats the firm as a social institution, calls for democratising it through worker election of management, and is democratic, in contrast to authoritarian or fascist corporatism.
scope: The democratic, non-authoritarian strand: John Stuart Mill's case for labourers' associations, the progressive-era 'interest group liberalism', and post-war societal neo-corporatism in Austria, the Netherlands, Germany and the Nordic states. Excludes fascist and Catholic-corporatist variants. Most social, cultural and foreign-policy questions are not addressed by the doctrine, so those answers are low-confidence inferences.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Liberal corporatism does not reject markets and Mill defends competition, but it adds organised coordination; markets are the base mechanism, not a claim of superiority over all government action.

public-ownership.rationale: Mill's ideal is workers' associations owning capital and the sources stress firms as social institutions in markets, not state ownership of industry.

unions-good.rationale: Strong labour unions are one of the 'social partners' in neo-corporatism and Mill treats worker associations as good for workers, though liberal corporatists want them integrated into bargaining rather than adversarial.

property-fundamental.rationale: Mill rejects confiscation yet foresees capital becoming joint property of workers; protection of property is accepted but not held as near-absolute, so split.

cut-welfare.rationale: The corporatist welfare states (Nordic, Austrian, Dutch) are comprehensive; the polder model supported an extensive welfare state even while trimming it.

worker-ownership.rationale: Mill expects labourers' associations collectively owning capital with elected managers to predominate, and liberal corporatism calls for democratising the firm; but some forms are non-socialist, so not strong.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: No documented position; European corporatist states often restrict it while the Millian liberal strand resists, so split.

strong-leader.rationale: Consensus bargaining among organised partners and coalition government (polder model) is the opposite of bypassing gridlock through one leader; neo-corporatism is defined against top-down fascist corporatism.

state-harmful.rationale: Neo-corporatism depends on the state recognising and working with social partners; it is a democratic, state-engaging model.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: No documented position; Dutch and German corporatist states legalise it but the doctrine itself is silent.

traditional-family.rationale: Catholic corporatism stressed family but liberal corporatism is secular-liberal and silent; split.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Some forms have nationalist-liberal traits (German State Party) but the mainstream is silent; split.

gradual-change.rationale: Consensus bargaining and incremental concertation (polder model) work through established institutions and avert disruption.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: No stated view; the model is organised nationally, though its states are often pro-EU, so split.

free-trade.rationale: Small open corporatist economies depend on trade; the polder article notes Dutch trade dependence ruled out protectionism.

limit-growth.rationale: Concertation aims at employment and growth (Wassenaar deal sought jobs); degrowth is not part of it.

revolution-justified.rationale: Liberal corporatism arose partly as a reaction against syndicalism and rests on consensus; Mill seeks a spontaneous, non-confiscatory transition.

experts-over-public.rationale: Polder concertation relied on expert planning advice (Central Planning Bureau) but is also organised democratic representation; split.

central-planning.rationale: Mill champions competition and liberal corporatism does not reject markets; it seeks bargaining within markets, not central planning.

socialized-markets.rationale: The doctrine accepts markets with firms run by or answerable to workers; Mill's co-operative associations compete in markets, though non-socialist forms exist.

land-value-tax.rationale: Mill favoured taxing unearned land increment, but the corporatist tradition is silent; split.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Mill favoured limiting inheritance but the doctrine is otherwise silent; split.

state-directs-investment.rationale: State intervention is minimal in sector bargaining; investment steering is not part of the model.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Mill favours wide worker ownership via associations, which broadly spreads property; but not the doctrine's focus.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The model is market based and Mill's associations still pay wages and profits; abolition is outside it.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Market-based but state-engaging systems; no support for abolishing state institutions.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Organised social partners bargain over economic policy and wages, with minimal state intervention; the statement adds state recognition and price-setting, which goes beyond what liberal corporatism specifies.

one-party-rule.rationale: Neo-corporatism is explicitly democratic as opposed to fascist or one-party state corporatism.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Constitutional monarchies (Netherlands, Nordics) host corporatist systems but the doctrine is indifferent; split.

democracy-best.rationale: Neo-corporatism is presented as a democratic form of corporatism; the doctrine also supplements majority rule, which keeps it from +2.

workers-councils.rationale: Workers should vote on management but political power stays with parliament; councils replacing parliaments is not the doctrine.

separate-church-state.rationale: Catholic corporatism influenced the broader tradition but the liberal strand is silent; split.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Liberal corporatism is a liberal-democratic doctrine; scriptural law is not part of any described version.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The model centres on state-recognised bodies and a state partner; privatising law and defence is far from it.

military-superiority.rationale: Small corporatist states such as the Netherlands and Nordics seldom claim superiority over rivals, but nothing in the doctrine decides it.

class-struggle-history.rationale: It replaces class conflict with cooperation between partners and arose as a reaction to syndicalism.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Nothing in liberal corporatism concerns indigenous land; adherents would be split along ordinary liberal lines.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Mill defends competition but also cooperation; split.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Corporatism stresses social roles of firms but liberal corporatism does not reject individualism.

human-enhancement.rationale: Not an issue the doctrine addresses; liberal adherents would split between freedom and caution.

direct-action.rationale: Concertation aims at averting strikes and disruption.

means-match-ends.rationale: Nothing stated; the doctrine's own practice is negotiated reform, but it makes no general claim about means and ends.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The doctrine resembles Taylorism with democratised management; division of labour assumed.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The doctrine does not reject markets, and Mill sees profit-sharing and partnership, not exploitation theory.

taxation-theft.rationale: Welfare-state corporatist systems rely on taxes and contributions.

harm-principle.rationale: Mill authored it but the corporatist tradition does not claim it; split.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Corporatism gives organised groups a representative role; rights are not individual only.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Voice through organised bargaining is the core mechanism.

state-as-business.rationale: Firms are social institutions; the state is not a business.

organic-representation.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale says liberal corporatism keeps parties and parliament, so the sources cited here do not support replacing parties as the basis of representation.

reviewHistory.rationale: Interest representation through trade bodies; but liberal corporatism keeps parties and parliament, so only agree.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Feudal personal fealty is the opposite of democratic, institutionalised partnership among representative bodies.

bound-labor.rationale: Mill rejects hereditary dependence of labour.

single-common-good.rationale: Corporatist bargaining balances organised interests rather than a single common good.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Not a question the doctrine addresses; adherents are split.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Not a question the doctrine addresses; adherents are split.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival is outside the doctrine; adherents are split.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Calls for democratisation of the firm and election of management by workers; Mill's managers elected and removable.

school-vouchers.rationale: Dutch and Nordic corporatist states fund private and religious schools, yet the doctrine takes no view on vouchers; split.

national-self-determination.rationale: Nationalist-liberal traits exist in some forms, but the doctrine has no stated position on nation-states.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Christian-democratic corporatists sit beside secular liberals, so adherents are split.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare is linked to contribution and residence in these states, but the doctrine does not address immigrants; split.

class-collaboration.rationale: Social partners cooperate; core of the doctrine.

dominated-front.rationale: Open, trade-dependent corporatist states are integrated with Western powers and would not join an anti-Western front.

workers-nation.rationale: The doctrine seeks class cooperation within the nation rather than organised class politics, national or international.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Neo-corporatism treats the state as one partner.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy supply is outside the doctrine; split by national circumstances.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Corporatist states differ greatly, from Dutch integration policy to Nordic multiculturalism; split.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist debate with no connection to the doctrine.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: A religious demand with no home in a liberal market-based doctrine.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Christian-democratic and secular strands of corporatism differ, as the Dutch pillarised schools show; split.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Leninist theory of the socialist state, opposed to the democratic character of neo-corporatism.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: A libertarian absolutism not held by corporatists, who accept state coercion for taxes and bargaining frameworks, though they are not militarists either; split.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Mill defends competition but social Darwinism not adopted; split.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Several corporatist democracies (Germany, Austria) have such laws while others do not; the doctrine takes no stance.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Mill's rejection of the employer-employed hierarchy resonates.

vanguard-party.rationale: Neo-corporatism is a democratic system of voluntary social partnership, and liberal corporatism arose against syndicalist and revolutionary currents, so a revolutionary leading party has no place.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Welfare-state corporatism protects workers broadly through insurance rather than giving the poor first priority; split.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Housing tenure is outside the doctrine; adherents split by party.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Concertation aims at avoiding strikes yet depends on union strength; split.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Corporatist bargaining sometimes fixes prices, but the doctrine favours markets; adherents split.

party-commands-army.rationale: A feature of authoritarian single-party states, contrary to neo-corporatism's democratic character.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Christian-democratic corporatism has Catholic roots but the liberal strand is indifferent to church governance.

clerical-rule.rationale: Religious rule contradicts the democratic liberal character of the doctrine.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: A Leninist slogan; corporatists seek class cooperation, including in wartime.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Mill's liberalism of free expression rejects moral censorship.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: A market-accepting doctrine has no basis for abolishing renting.

people-in-arms.rationale: Replacing professional forces with an armed citizenry is alien to this institutional doctrine.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: No documented view; adherents split between relativist and universalist liberals.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Corporatist states vary (Germany versus Netherlands); the doctrine has no view.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Mill authored this; the corporatist tradition silent.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Neo-corporatism is explicitly democratic as opposed to authoritarian state corporatism.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A left-theoretical debate unconnected to the doctrine.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Sacred rulers belong to the pre-liberal and fascist traditions that neo-corporatism rejects.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The model is democratic, rule-of-law and constitutional.

leader-cult.rationale: A fascist-corporatist trait; neo-corporatism is the democratic contrast.

women-must-cover.rationale: Mill's liberty principle makes the demand contrary to liberal values.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The sources give no view on minority emigration versus struggle for rights; adherents split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Open trade dependence is a precondition of the Dutch consensus model.

moral-incentives.rationale: The doctrine accepts markets and material incentives.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Opposed to revolution and armed vanguards; the model is consensual.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Curriculum content is outside a doctrine about economic bargaining; adherents split.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Mill held a paternalist view but modern adherents; split.

patriotic-education.rationale: Some forms have nationalist-liberal traits but the mainstream strand takes no view on patriotic schooling.

public-money-creation.rationale: A market-accepting doctrine has no stated case for public money creation.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Doctrine premised on adapting capitalism by bargaining.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: A post-colonial question outside the doctrine; adherents split.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The doctrine assigns duties to firms as social institutions, but not a paternalist duty of the wealthy; split.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The model relies on citizens organising into representative bodies.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Not part of a liberal-market doctrine.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: The doctrine rejects the ruling-class model of the state.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Revanchism is contrary to the consensual model.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Neo-corporatism defines itself against fascist corporatism but takes no stated view on equating fascism with communism.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: A culture-war question the doctrine does not address; adherents split.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Gender policy is outside the doctrine; adherents split.

paid-care-work.rationale: Nordic states fund care services but the doctrine itself does not address paying domestic work.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: A legal-theory question outside the doctrine; adherents split.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The doctrine accepts markets without judging consumption; adherents split.

corporate-influence.rationale: Interest group liberalism accepts group lobbying; split.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Nordic family policy includes such incentives but the doctrine takes no view; split.

job-guarantee.rationale: Nordic active labour-market policy resembles it but the doctrine is silent.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Conspiracy claims are contrary to the democratic liberal tradition.

informal-organisation.rationale: Opposed to informal organisation: organised, licensed bodies.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on accepting or rejecting common ownership of production, or on private property in general, and the statement now asks only whether personal belongings should stay private where production is held in common.

reviewHistory.rationale: Property in means of production is accepted in markets, and personal property is not in dispute, so there is no meaningful stance.

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on accepting or rejecting common ownership of production, or on private property in general, and the statement now asks only whether personal belongings should stay private where production is held in common.

socialized-care.rationale: Nordic public care exists but the doctrine is silent.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Linguistic purism has no place in an open, trade-oriented liberal doctrine, so adherents lean disagree.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Mill favours cooperatives within markets rather than communities of common property.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Corporatism often presents itself as a third way.

holocaust-denial.rationale: A factual claim rejected by liberal-democratic adherents.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Neo-corporatism is democratic, opposed to authoritarian suppression.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Contrary to Mill's freedom of opinion.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: A religious-legal question outside liberal corporatism.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: A critical-theory claim the doctrine does not address; adherents split.

assisted-dying.rationale: A bioethical question with no basis in the doctrine; Dutch law permits it but adherents differ.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxian concept; the doctrine's democratisation of the firm responds to similar concerns but is not framed that way.

social-market-economy.rationale: Germany's social market economy is listed as a neo-corporatist form.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Corporatist states are split between NATO members and neutrals such as Austria and Sweden historically.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a constitutional or ceremonial crown, and the statement now asks only about passing real governing power to a child.

reviewHistory.rationale: Constitutional monarchies host corporatism but are indifferent.

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a constitutional or ceremonial crown, and the statement now asks only about passing real governing power to a child.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Doctrine is silent on religious reform; adherents split.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The model relies on state institutions.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Corporatist welfare states provide aid through public social insurance.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Internal church governance is outside the doctrine; adherents split.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Mill's profit sharing rewards labour; unclear.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The consensus-seeking, interest-bargaining view treats politics as negotiation, not a struggle between good and evil.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The doctrine is partly non-socialist, and the question belongs to socialist debates.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Nordic and Dutch states often run local utilities publicly, but the doctrine takes no stance.

family-wage.rationale: Union-bargained family wages were part of mid-century corporatist deals, but the doctrine does not state it; split.

person-over-state.rationale: Mill's liberalism gives primacy to persons; liberal corporatism does not reject individualism, per its Wikipedia description.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Christian-democratic and secular strands differ; no common view.

free-public-college.rationale: Nordic states offer it but the doctrine does not address tuition.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Collective bargaining is the core mechanism; sector bargaining central.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Neo-corporatism needs a functioning state as one of the partners in tripartite bargaining, so smashing it is the opposite of the model.

public-service-media.rationale: Dutch and Nordic states fund public broadcasters, but the doctrine is silent on media policy.

voter-id.rationale: The doctrine does not address election rules; adherents in the Nordic, Dutch and Austrian systems differ on this.

women-suffrage.rationale: Liberal corporatism is democratic and liberal, and the Nordic, Dutch and Austrian systems it describes grant women full political rights; Mill also argued for it.

indirect-election.rationale: Its social-partner bodies use delegated representation, but the doctrine does not address election of higher offices; adherents are split.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Liberal corporatism is democratic and keeps individual liberty, in contrast to authoritarian corporatism, so killing without trial is rejected.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: The doctrine rests on bargaining among employers, workers and the state as organised social partners, so bypassing interest groups contradicts it.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Dutch pillarisation was denominational while other corporatist states were not, so the sources give no single answer.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Mill rejects confiscation, which points toward process, but corporatist welfare states also seek equality; adherents split.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Liberal corporatism keeps a market economy within a democratic system and is contrasted with authoritarian forms, so one-party communist rule is rejected.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The corporatist welfare states (Nordic, Austrian, Dutch) are comprehensive; the polder model supported an extensive welfare state even while trimming it. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Employers' associations and trade unions should negotiate pay and economic policy at sector or national level with the government as a partner.
missingStatements.rationale: This tripartite or sector bargaining is the central mechanism of neo-corporatism.

missingStatements.text: Firms should be run as social institutions that answer to their workers as well as their owners.
missingStatements.rationale: Liberal corporatism treats the firm as a social institution that must recognise members' needs.

notes: Wikipedia's article is a short stub, so documented positions concentrate on economic organisation; most other answers are inferred from the liberal-democratic character of the corporatist states.
